section.title: Manage Remote Repositories
section.p: Use: Opens a dialog box where you can add, edit, or delete remote repositories for the current working copy.

Details: A remote repository is a named location, usually on a server, that the local repository uses for push and pull operations. The most common remote name is origin. Use this action to update remote URLs, add another remote, or remove a remote that is no longer used.

section.title: Edit Repository Config File
section.p: Use: Opens the repository configuration file in the main editor.

Details: The repository configuration file stores local Git settings for the current repository, such as remote URLs, branch tracking settings, and repository-specific options. Changes made in this file affect the current repository, not all repositories on your system.
Caution: Edit the repository configuration file only if you know which Git settings you need to change. Incorrect values can affect push, pull, branch tracking, or other repository behavior.

section.title: Preferences
section.p: Use: Opens the Git Client preferences page.

Details: The preferences page contains Git Client settings that can affect all repositories or the current project, depending on the setting. Use it to configure behavior such as authentication, commit signing, and other Git Client options.
Scope: Global or project-level Git Client settings.

section.title: Reset All Credentials
section.p: Use: Removes stored credentials so that the Git Client prompts you for new credentials when authentication is needed again.

Details: Stored credentials can include usernames, passwords, tokens, or other authentication data used to connect to remote repositories. Resetting them does not change the repository history or remote configuration. It only removes saved authentication data used by the Git Client.
Best Practice: Use this action when saved credentials are no longer valid, when access tokens were rotated, or when you need to authenticate with different credentials.
